text: This walkthrough presents a PhD proposal from Universiti Malaya: estimating atrial ectopy from smartwatch beat intervals after stroke. Excessive supraventricular ectopic activity, or ESVEA, helps decide which stroke survivors get prolonged rhythm monitoring. But every ESVEA threshold was derived on Holter ECG, the very resource being rationed. Smartwatches report beat-to-beat intervals with a per-beat quality flag, yet nobody knows the error of a daily ectopic count built from them. Two problems stand out. Filtering removes ectopic beats preferentially, and the data a watch keeps are weighted towards the night, while premature atrial contractions, or PACs, peak in the afternoon and evening.

The study asks four questions. First, how much ectopy information is lost when a pulse waveform becomes a quality-filtered interval series. Second, whether a two-scale spatio-temporal graph neural network, using the quality flag as input, estimates the ectopy rate better than non-graph baselines. Third, whether a seven-day smartwatch protocol after stroke yields enough usable data. And fourth, whether substituting the smartwatch estimate for the ECG count changes ESVEA classification. The primary definition of ESVEA is four hundred and eighty or more supraventricular beats per day.

The four objectives form a dependency chain. Icentia11k, a large ECG dataset with beat labels, supplies truth for the information-loss analysis, for model training, and for a held-out substitution test. Pulsewatch, which pairs wrist pulse signals, motion and reference ECG, supplies the motion term of the retention model. The Garmin specification fixes how flags and gaps behave. Objective one feeds the model design, the frozen model feeds the substitution test, and the stroke cohort feeds deployability and the real-world coverage profile. If the cohort cannot start in time, objectives one, two and four still proceed.

Objective one starts with filtering. A common rule rejects any interval that deviates from the median of the five preceding accepted intervals by more than a threshold, usually twenty percent. A premature beat is short by definition, and its pause is long, so both are rejected. In this illustrative series you can see the band around the running reference and the crosses on rejected intervals.

On two hundred and ninety-eight Icentia11k patients, the effect is large. At the common twenty percent threshold, the filter removed sixty-one percent of PAC coupling intervals but only nine percent of normal intervals. And the loss depends on burden: patients with ESVEA lose a smaller share of their PAC intervals than patients without it, probably because frequent PACs enter the running reference and are then accepted. So a single correction factor is unlikely to restore the count. Hypothesis one tests this at patient level, in new patients.

Objective two builds the estimator. The model works at two scales. At the beat scale, the stream of reported beats is cut into windows of N beats, so a gap shortens the day rather than creating empty windows. An attention readout pools each window into one embedding, giving more weight to informative beats such as a PAC and its pause. At the epoch scale, the window embeddings form a graph across the day, processed by graph convolution and a selective state-space layer. Because Icentia11k segments have no clock time, training uses pseudo-days built from one patient's segments.

Inside each window there are two graphs. The temporal chain links each beat to its neighbours in time, capturing the short-then-long signature of a premature beat. The similarity graph links each beat to its k nearest neighbours in feature space, so recurring PACs share evidence wherever they occur. Both graphs are built once per window and reused in every layer.

One local layer sums three branches: the chain neighbours scaled by a learned gate alpha, the beat's own features, and the similarity neighbours scaled by a learned gate beta. The sum is normalised and passed through a ReLU. The self branch keeps a single premature beat from being averaged away, and because alpha and beta are reported, the weight given to each kind of evidence can be inspected. Every component is then tested against simpler alternatives by ablation.

The Garmin quality flag marks both motion-affected beats and any interval it judges abnormally short or long, so a premature beat tends to be flagged. Deleting flagged beats would delete the very events being counted. Instead, the flag enters the model as an input. Each kind of loss then goes to one place: flagged beats stay as input, marked gaps go to observed time, beats silently missed at motion are corrected by inverse retention weighting, and a premature beat with no wrist pulse cannot be corrected and is measured instead.

Equation 3.1 defines retention, pi hat of m: the probability that a beat outside a gap is reported at motion level m, fitted on Pulsewatch. Equation 3.2 turns calibrated beat probabilities into a daily rate. Each reported beat is weighted by one over its retention, each six-hour block is divided by its own observed hours, and the four blocks are combined by length, so a night-heavy recording no longer biases the day. This revised form of Equation 3.1 awaits supervisor confirmation.

This worked example uses illustrative numbers. Most observed time falls at night and most ectopy in the afternoon and evening. The naive count divides all PACs by all observed hours. Retention weighting raises it. Block weighting then gives each six-hour block a quarter of the day, however few hours were observed in it. Equation 3.3, the coverage gate, reports the daily value only if every block reaches a minimum of observed hours; otherwise the model abstains.

Over a week, single days often abstain. Here day two and day seven fail the gate, day five was not worn, and day six clears every block but fails the day and night validity rule, so it also abstains. ESVEA status therefore uses Equation 3.4, which pools each block across valid days. In the simulation in Appendix C, under poor coverage, pooling kept the count computable for about eighty-eight percent of participants, against about eighty-one percent for the per-day rule, with lower misclassification.

Evaluation keeps patients apart. Icentia11k is split into four disjoint sets: P zero for the preliminary analysis, P one for the hypothesis one test, P two for model development, and P three, held out untouched until the model is frozen at milestone M4. Hypothesis two is the single primary contrast: the graph model against the best non-graph baseline, on the mean absolute error of the daily-equivalent count, with a paired subject-level bootstrap. In objective four, the held-out patients are degraded with flags, gaps, pulse deficit and timing noise, and the frozen model's ESVEA calls are compared with the ECG reference.

Objective three recruits about forty adults after ischaemic stroke or TIA for seven days of Garmin wear. The primary outcome is the proportion with at least three valid days, with a traffic-light rule: green at seventy-five percent or more, red at fifty or below. Device verification on non-participant wear comes first, including twenty-four-hour interval logging, which Garmin has so far confirmed only by personal communication.

Preliminary evidence from a cross-device pilot shows that the interval representation carries rhythm information. Ranking transferred across devices, with AUROC of 0.995 or higher wherever non-AF windows existed. But the operating point did not transfer: AF recall fell to forty-five percent on MIMIC-III fingertip signals. Each external cohort has only one AF subject, so these results show feasibility, not accuracy. These pilot values await supervisor confirmation.

A pre-registered Pulsewatch check in eight subjects found beat matching well above chance at high motion, falling from 0.85 to 0.41 as motion rose. But absolute retention depended on the peak detector, so the check did not pass and no retention value is claimed. The estimate will be reported with a detector sensitivity analysis.

To close, the limits are stated plainly. Error is characterised on ECG-labelled data under simulated losses, not on a real device. Pulse deficit cannot be corrected by weighting, so its bias is measured. Transfer from Samsung to Garmin is an assumption. The contribution is the observation model: the flag as evidence, a frozen retention correction, and a coverage gate that knows when not to report. The graph architecture is a means, tested against baselines, not the claim itself.
